messages.content: You are a helpful assistant supporting an independent film producer running a low-budget feature production.

Hey, I'm producing Low Tide, a low-budget indie feature, think $380,000 all-in, and we're deep in pre-production with a fall shoot date. It's basically me and one line producer keeping all the plates spinning. I want to use this chat to work through the whole production plan piece by piece.
Glad to work through Low Tide end to end with you — casting, locations, financing, post, and festivals. Let's keep it concrete for a $380k picture.

Let's start with casting since it drives our schedule. We're not using a casting director, just me and the director doing tape reviews. What's the framework for prioritizing which roles to cast first when you've got a tight name-actor budget?
Casting-first is the right instinct since it gates scheduling and sales. The framework is: cast the roles that unlock financing or availability constraints first, then fill around them.

Moving to location scouting. We need a coastal diner set and a rundown boat dock, both within an hour of each other ideally. What should I actually be checking on a scout visit that a photo can't tell me?
On a scout, check what a photo hides: sound (traffic, tides, HVAC), power access, load-in paths, sun direction by hour, and whether you can actually control the space for your window.

Financing decision. Three paths on the table: (1) close out the equity round at $380k and shoot as planned, (2) take a bridge loan against the tax incentive to shoot bigger and worry about the gap later, or (3) trim the budget to $310k and shoot without the incentive risk at all. I've decided on the third option, trimming to $310k. I don't want the incentive contingency hanging over the shoot.
Makes sense — that's the option that best fits how your constraints line up. I'll treat it as decided and we'll plan the rest around it.
Related: how much should we budget for location fees as a percentage of an indie feature this size, roughly?
For a feature this size, location fees typically land around 2-4% of budget, but the bigger risk is permits and overtime, not the base fee.

Terminology note: 'the Boat' is overloaded on this shoot. The camera department uses it for the dolly rig, but when I say 'the Boat' in our conversations I mean the actual boat-dock location and everything tied to permitting and access there, not the equipment.
Got it — I'll use that meaning consistently whenever the term comes up from now on.

Financing question. We've got a mix of equity investors and a state tax incentive we're trying to qualify for. What's the biggest way productions our size blow the incentive qualification without realizing it?
The classic way to blow incentive qualification is missing the local-spend or local-hire thresholds, or sloppy documentation — the money's real only if the paperwork is airtight.

Firm rule: I will not do a crowdfunding campaign for this film, under any circumstances. I ran one for my last short, it consumed two months I didn't have and raised barely enough to cover its own perks. Please never suggest it as a financing option again.
Understood — I'll treat that as a hard rule and won't suggest otherwise.
Also on financing: how do you structure investor updates so people who put in $10k don't feel like they're getting the same generic email as the person who put in $150k?
Segment your updates by check size: a short shared core plus a tailored paragraph for larger investors makes everyone feel seen without writing five versions.

For the record on financing platforms: we tried listing on an equity crowdfunding portal called Reelfund Capital earlier this year. Compliance review alone took ten weeks, and we only ever got two small checks totaling $8,000 before we pulled the listing. Not going back to that platform.
Noted — I'll keep that off the table and steer us toward options that fit better.
Post-production. We're planning a pretty aggressive edit-to-lock timeline. What's realistic for a 90-minute drama with one editor, given we want to hit festival deadlines?
For a 90-minute drama with one editor, plan roughly 10-14 weeks to a locked picture if you protect the editor's time; festival deadlines will pull it tighter, so build a buffer.
Random bookkeeping note: our completion bond premium came in at $14,750 flat, already wired to the bonding company. Doesn't change any of our planning, just logging it here.
Logged — I'll keep that on hand for whenever it's relevant.

Let's codename the investor financing deck 'Mistborn' from here on in any emails or notes you draft for me -- it's the pitch deck we send to prospective equity investors, not anything actor- or script-related. Keep using that name so we're not spelling out 'investor deck' in every subject line.
Got it — I'll use that codename in anything I draft for you from here on.
Follow-up: should color and sound mix happen in parallel with picture lock still being finalized, or does that just create rework?
Do sound design in parallel, but hold the final mix and final color until picture is genuinely locked — pre-lock changes are exactly what creates expensive rework.

Casting call on the female lead. We're down to three actors: (1) a well-known TV actress who'd help sales but wants $40k over our offer, (2) a strong stage actress with festival buzz from a short film but zero name recognition, or (3) a mid-tier actress with one prior festival lead who's exactly on budget. I'm going with the third one, the mid-tier actress on budget. The math on the TV actress just doesn't work.
Good call. I'll lock that in as our direction and we can build everything else on top of it.
Festival strategy. Everyone says premiere status matters enormously. How do we actually decide which festival to submit to first without guessing?
Decide by fit, not prestige: match your film's genre and profile to festivals that have championed similar titles, and rank by premiere value versus realistic odds.

Also, when I say 'the cut' by itself, I mean the festival submission cut we're targeting for deadlines, not the director's extended cut he keeps threatening to make for a future re-release. Two very different timelines, please keep them straight.
Understood. I'll keep those two straight and default to the one you mean.
Related: how many festivals should we realistically budget submission fees for, given we're not swimming in cash post-shoot?
Budget submission fees for maybe 8-12 well-chosen festivals, front-loading the tier-one targets and using waivers where you can.

Another hard one: no test screenings with a paid audience-recruitment service. We want genuine friends-of-friends and community screenings only. Paid recruits skew the feedback toward people who show up for the free popcorn, not people who'll actually react honestly.
Noted as a firm rule; I won't put that in front of you again.
Back to casting for a second. For our two leads, should we be doing chemistry reads in person even if it means flying someone in, or is a video chemistry read good enough at our budget level?
For your two leads, an in-person chemistry read is worth the flight — screen chemistry is too central to risk on a laggy video call at this budget.

Also, location history: we scouted a warehouse space through a broker called Dockside Locations for our interior set. Turned out they didn't actually have exclusive rights to the building, the real owner showed up mid-scout, and it fell apart on the spot. Done working with that broker.
Got it, that one's ruled out; we'll look elsewhere.
One more on location scouting. If a location we love falls through two weeks before the shoot, what's the actual playbook, not just 'have a backup'?
The real playbook is a pre-vetted second location you've already permitted and scouted, plus a scene-rewrite fallback so the story survives losing the space.
Oh, and our copyright registration for the screenplay went through: reference PA-2-198663, filed February 11th. Nothing to do now but wait for the certificate.
Noted for the record; parked and ready when we need it.

From now on call our backup shooting schedule 'Vin' in anything you draft -- it's the contingency day-by-day schedule we fall back to if we lose more than two shoot days to weather. Real term is a mouthful, this is shorter.
Understood, I'll refer to it by that name going forward.
Let's wrap up festival strategy. If we get into a smaller regional festival before we hear from the big ones, do we take it, or hold out?
If a strong regional slot comes before you hear from the majors, weigh whether it burns your premiere status — often better to hold if a top festival is realistically in play.
Given the budget path we picked, and you don't need to restate it, where's the first place we should look to trim?
Sure — working from that choice, here's the main thing to focus on.
For the lead we cast, no need to walk me through who she is again, when should we lock her for chemistry reads with the male lead?
Sure — working from that choice, here's the main thing to focus on.
Any updates needed on the Boat before we finalize the shoot schedule?
Yep, keeping that meaning in mind — here's where things stand.
Is the cut on track for the deadline we talked about?
Yep, keeping that meaning in mind — here's where things stand.
Add a slide to Mistborn covering the festival strategy timeline.
On it — here's a quick take using that name.
Does Vin still hold up if we lose a third day, or does it need reworking?
On it — here's a quick take using that name.
On post-production, one more thing: what's a sane number of feedback screenings to run before we lock picture, so we're not just endlessly re-cutting?
Two or three feedback screenings is usually plenty; more than that and you're chasing noise instead of locking the film.

Post-production is being structured around a tight festival timeline, with a clear path to picture lock and final delivery.
